The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$, $m\in\mathbb R^d$, and let $\Sigma$ be a real symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then its law has Lebesgue density
$$f_{m,\Sigma}(x)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}\det(\Sigma)^{-1/2} \exp\!\left(-\tfrac12(x-m)^T\Sigma^{-1}(x-m)\right), \qquad x\in\mathbb R^d.$$

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
([[def-probability-measure]]). Absolute continuity $P\ll Q$ has the convention
of [[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]. If
$P\not\ll Q$, define $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$. If $P\ll Q$, assume AC
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) as in [[def-likelihood-ratio-as-rn-derivative]] and
let $r=dP/dQ$ be a finite-valued nonnegative measurable representative of its
Radon–Nikodym class; such a representative exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].
On $\{r=0\}$ set $\ell=0$, and on $\{r>0\}$ set $\ell=\log r$. This
function is measurable: for $a\ge0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r>\exp(a)\}$, and for
$a<0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r=0\}\cup\{r>\exp(a)\}$, by the inverse and
monotonicity properties of the natural logarithm
([[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]). These are
measurable sets by [[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Since
$P(\{r=0\})=\int_{\{r=0\}}r\,dQ=0$ by
[[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]], the value chosen there does not
affect $\int\ell\,dP$. Define
$$D(P\|Q):=\int \ell\,dP,$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm ([[def-natural-logarithm]]).

The definition is independent of the representative: two representatives
agree $Q$-almost everywhere, hence $P$-almost everywhere. Put
$$\psi(0):=0,\qquad \psi(t):=t\log t\quad(t>0).$$
The function $\psi$ is continuous at zero: for $s\ge1$,
$$0\le \frac{\log s}{s}=\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{u}\le\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{\sqrt u}\le\frac2{\sqrt s}.$$
Thus $t\log t\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$; here $L=\log$ by
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]] and
[[def-integral-logarithm]]. On $(0,\infty)$, $\psi$ is a product of continuous
functions by [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], so $\psi$ is continuous on
$[0,\infty)$ and $\psi(r)$ is measurable by
[[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Its signed integral is
defined by the positive and negative parts
([[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]],
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

For $0<t\le1$, the function $-t\log t$ has derivative $-\log t-1$ and
maximum $1/e$ at $t=1/e$: $e=\exp(1)>1$ by
[[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], $1/e=\exp(-1)$ by
[[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], and $\log(1/e)=-1$ by
[[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and the inverse definition. The mean value
theorem gives increase before and decrease after this point
([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-integral-logarithm-derivative-and-normalisation]],
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]], [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).
At $t=0$ the negative part is zero. Since $Q$ is a probability measure,
$$\int \psi(r)^-\,dQ\le\frac1e.$$
The change-of-measure identity of [[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]],
applied to $\ell^-$ gives $\int\ell^-\,dP=\int\psi(r)^-\,dQ\le1/e$,
so $\int\ell\,dP$ is well-defined; applying it to both positive and negative
parts gives
$$D(P\|Q)=\int\ell\,dP=\int\psi(r)\,dQ=\int r\log r\,dQ,$$
with $0\log0:=0$ and a finite negative part. Therefore the extended integral
is well-defined without an $\infty-\infty$ ambiguity.

This convention is directional: the first argument must be absolutely
continuous with respect to the second for the integral formula to apply.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Let $d,T\ge1$ be finite integers, let $I_d$ be the $d\times d$ identity matrix, and let $\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_T\in(0,1)$. Set $\alpha_t=1-\beta_t$, $\bar\alpha_0=1$, and $\bar\alpha_t=\prod_{s=1}^t\alpha_s$. Write $\lambda_d$ for Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R^d$ and define, for $v>0$,
$$\phi_{d,v}(y;m)=(2\pi v)^{-d/2}\exp\!\left(-\frac{\|y-m\|_2^2}{2v}\right),\qquad y,m\in\mathbb R^d.$$
The notation $\|z\|_2^2=\sum_{i=1}^d z_i^2$ is the squared Euclidean norm. The displayed function is the Lebesgue density of $N_d(m,vI_d)$.

For each fixed $x_0\in\mathbb R^d$, the forward chain has path density on $(\mathbb R^d)^T$
$$q(x_{1:T}\mid x_0)=\prod_{t=1}^T \phi_{d,\beta_t}(x_t;\sqrt{\alpha_t}\,x_{t-1}).$$
Thus its transition from $x_{t-1}$ to $x_t$ is Gaussian with mean $\sqrt{\alpha_t}\,x_{t-1}$ and covariance $\beta_t I_d$. Each factor is a normalized density, and finite successive integration of the nonnegative product gives a probability density.

For a generic adjacent pair, the two model directions are shown below. The arrows indicate the direction in which each conditional density generates its target state; they assert no equality or inverse relation between the kernels.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=stealth]
  \node (previous) at (0,0) {$x_{t-1}$};
  \node (current) at (4,0) {$x_t$};
  \draw[->] (previous) to[bend left=24] node[midway,above] {$q(x_t\mid x_{t-1})$} (current);
  \draw[->] (current) to[bend left=24] node[midway,below] {$p_{\theta,t}(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)$} (previous);
\end{tikzpicture}
```

A learned reverse Gaussian model consists of finite-valued Borel maps $\mu_{\theta,t}:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ and fixed variances $\sigma_t^2\in(0,\infty)$, for $1\le t\le T$. It is the joint density
$$p_\theta(x_{0:T})=\phi_{d,1}(x_T;0)\prod_{t=1}^T\phi_{d,\sigma_t^2}(x_{t-1};\mu_{\theta,t}(x_t)).$$
Its prior is $p(x_T)=N_d(0,I_d)$, and its marginal density at $x_0$ is
$$p_\theta(x_0)=\int_{(\mathbb R^d)^T}p_\theta(x_{0:T})\,d\lambda_d(x_1)\cdots d\lambda_d(x_T),$$
whenever this integral is finite. The joint reverse density is normalized by successive integration of its Gaussian transition factors followed by the prior density.

For $t=1$, the forward-chain conditional $q(x_0\mid x_1,x_0)$ assigns probability one to every Borel set containing $x_0$ and zero to every Borel set not containing $x_0$; it is not a Lebesgue density. The separate learned reverse likelihood $p_\theta(x_0\mid x_1)$ is the Gaussian density above with variance $\sigma_1^2>0$.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $m\ge1$ be finite, let $d_j\ge1$, and let
$Z_j$ for $1\le j\le m$ be mutually independent random elements of
$\mathbb R^{d_j}$. Suppose $Z_j\sim N_{d_j}(a_j,\Sigma_j)$, where each
$\Sigma_j$ is symmetric positive semidefinite. Put
$D=\sum_{j=1}^m d_j$, $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m)$,
$a=(a_1,\ldots,a_m)$, and
$\Sigma=\operatorname{diag}(\Sigma_1,\ldots,\Sigma_m)$. Then
$$Z\sim N_D(a,\Sigma).$$
No covariance block needs to be invertible.

Assume AC. Let $X\in\mathbb R^d$ and $Y\in\mathbb R^m$, with $d,m\ge1$, be
jointly multivariate normal with mean $(a,b)$ and positive-semidefinite block
covariance
$$\Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}A&C\\C^T&B\end{pmatrix},$$
where $B$ is positive definite. Then
$$S=A-CB^{-1}C^T$$
is positive semidefinite, and for every $y\in\mathbb R^m$ the probability law
$$K(y,\cdot)=N_d\!\left(a+CB^{-1}(y-b),S\right)$$
is defined. The map $K$ is a probability kernel and is a conditional law of
$X$ given $Y$: for all Borel $E\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ and
$F\subseteq\mathbb R^m$,
$$\mathbb P(X\in E,Y\in F)=\int_F K(y,E)\,\mathbb P_Y(dy).$$
The covariance $A$ and the conditional covariance $S$ may be singular.
Positive definiteness of $B$ is required; no pseudoinverse formula for
singular $B$ is asserted.

derivations.claim: Under the forward path law with fixed $x_0$, for each $s$ put $\xi_s=(X_s-\sqrt{\alpha_s}X_{s-1})/\sqrt{\beta_s}$. Changing variables $x_s=\sqrt{\alpha_s}x_{s-1}+\sqrt{\beta_s}z$ in the last transition density in [F1] gives the conditional density $\phi_{d,1}(z;0)$, independent of the past. Thus for Borel past events $A$ and Borel $B\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, $\mathbb P(X_{1:s-1}\in A,\xi_s\in B)=\mathbb P(X_{1:s-1}\in A)N_d(0,I_d)(B)$. Each $\xi_s$ is standard Gaussian and independent of the previous path; since earlier innovations are measurable functions of that path, $\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_t$ are mutually independent for every $t$.

Iterating $X_t=\sqrt{\alpha_t}X_{t-1}+\sqrt{\beta_t}\xi_t$ gives $X_t=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0+\sum_{s=1}^t\sqrt{\beta_s\prod_{r=s+1}^t\alpha_r}\,\xi_s$. By step 1.1 and [F3], the finite innovation stack is jointly Gaussian. Thus each scalar projection of $X_t$ is normal with mean $u\cdot\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0$ and, by independence, variance $u^T\left(\sum_{s=1}^t\beta_s\prod_{r=s+1}^t\alpha_r I_d\right)u$; [F2] identifies its law as multivariate normal with that mean and covariance. Since $\beta_s\prod_{r=s+1}^t\alpha_r=\prod_{r=s+1}^t\alpha_r-\prod_{r=s}^t\alpha_r$, the covariance sum telescopes to $(1-\bar\alpha_t)I_d$.

Fix $t\ge2$. By step 2.1, $X_{t-1}$ is Gaussian, and by step 1.1, $\xi_t$ is independent of the past and standard Gaussian. The finite-stack result [F3] makes $(X_{t-1},\xi_t)$ jointly Gaussian. For any $u,v\in\mathbb R^d$, the projection of $(X_{t-1},X_t)$ is $(u+\sqrt{\alpha_t}v)\cdot X_{t-1}+\sqrt{\beta_t}v\cdot\xi_t$, a scalar projection of that Gaussian stack; hence [F2] makes the pair jointly Gaussian. Its means are $\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}x_0$ and $\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0$, and its covariance blocks are $A=(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})I_d$, $C=\sqrt{\alpha_t}(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})I_d$, and $B=(1-\bar\alpha_t)I_d$. The full block covariance is positive semidefinite because each of its quadratic forms is the variance of a scalar projection of $(X_{t-1},X_t)$. Since $0<\alpha_s<1$, we have $0<\bar\alpha_t<1$, so $B$ is positive definite.

Applying [F4] with these blocks gives conditional covariance $A-CB^{-1}C^T=\left((1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})-\frac{\alpha_t(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})^2}{1-\bar\alpha_t}\right)I_d=\frac{\beta_t(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})}{1-\bar\alpha_t}I_d$ and conditional mean $\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}x_0+\frac{\sqrt{\alpha_t}(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})}{1-\bar\alpha_t}(x_t-\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0)=\frac{\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}\beta_t}{1-\bar\alpha_t}x_0+\frac{\sqrt{\alpha_t}(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})}{1-\bar\alpha_t}x_t$. For $t\ge2$, $\bar\alpha_{t-1}<1$ and $\beta_t>0$, so $\tilde\beta_t>0$. This is the asserted conditional law; no density for the degenerate $t=1$ conditional was used.

The normalization follows from positive-scalar homogeneity of the nonnegative integral:
$$\int\pi\,d\mu=Z^{-1}\int\gamma\,d\mu=1.$$

Define the normalized target density $\pi:=\gamma/Z$. Then $\int\pi\,d\mu=1$. For a measurable probability density $q\ge0$ (that is, $\int_\Omega q\,d\mu=1$), write $q\ll_\mu\pi$ to mean $q=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $\{\pi=0\}$. This is a support condition on the two densities. It ensures that the induced probability measures $Q:=q\,\mu$ and $\Pi:=\pi\,\mu$ have $Q\ll\Pi$.

The normalization follows from positive-scalar homogeneity of the nonnegative integral:
$$\int\pi\,d\mu=Z^{-1}\int\gamma\,d\mu=1.$$
The induced density set functions are measures by [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]]. Their total masses are one: $Q(\Omega)=1$ by the probability-density hypothesis on $q$, and $\Pi(\Omega)=1$ by the preceding calculation. The support condition then gives $q=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $A$, and hence $Q(A)=0$. The homogeneity and zero-integral criteria used here are [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]] and [[thm-nonnegative-integral-zero-iff-zero-almost-everywhere]].

Let $\mu,\gamma,Z,\pi,q$ satisfy [[def-variational-family-and-elbo]], and put $Q=q\,\mu$ and $\Pi=\pi\,\mu$. The choice-free density-ratio identity
$$\log Z=\operatorname{ELBO}(q)+\int q\log(q/\pi)\,d\mu$$
holds, with the ratio integrand set to zero where $q=0$. Under AC, the final integral is the library reverse divergence $D(Q\|\Pi)$ and is nonnegative. Consequently
$$\operatorname{ELBO}(q)\le\log Z.$$

Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$, $m,n\in\mathbb R^d$, and $v,w>0$. If $Q=N_d(m,vI_d)$ and $P=N_d(n,wI_d)$, then
$$D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q\|P)=\frac d2\left(\frac vw-1+\log\frac wv\right)+\frac{\|m-n\|_2^2}{2w},$$
where the KL divergence is directional, its first argument is absolutely continuous with respect to its second, and $\log$ is the natural logarithm.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element. Its
**law** or **distribution** is the set function
$$\mathbb P_X:\Sigma\to[0,+\infty],\qquad \mathbb P_X(B):=\mathbb P(X^{-1}(B)).$$

Thus the law of $X$ records the probability of each measurable target set by
pulling it back to an event in the original probability space.

Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
([[def-probability-measure]]). Absolute continuity $P\ll Q$ has the convention
of [[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]. If
$P\not\ll Q$, define $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$. If $P\ll Q$, assume AC
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) as in [[def-likelihood-ratio-as-rn-derivative]] and
let $r=dP/dQ$ be a finite-valued nonnegative measurable representative of its
Radon–Nikodym class; such a representative exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].
On $\{r=0\}$ set $\ell=0$, and on $\{r>0\}$ set $\ell=\log r$. This
function is measurable: for $a\ge0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r>\exp(a)\}$, and for
$a<0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r=0\}\cup\{r>\exp(a)\}$, by the inverse and
monotonicity properties of the natural logarithm
([[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]). These are
measurable sets by [[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Since
$P(\{r=0\})=\int_{\{r=0\}}r\,dQ=0$ by
[[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]], the value chosen there does not
affect $\int\ell\,dP$. Define
$$D(P\|Q):=\int \ell\,dP,$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm ([[def-natural-logarithm]]).

The definition is independent of the representative: two representatives
agree $Q$-almost everywhere, hence $P$-almost everywhere. Put
$$\psi(0):=0,\qquad \psi(t):=t\log t\quad(t>0).$$
The function $\psi$ is continuous at zero: for $s\ge1$,

[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]] and
[[def-integral-logarithm]]. On $(0,\infty)$, $\psi$ is a product of continuous
functions by [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], so $\psi$ is continuous on
$[0,\infty)$ and $\psi(r)$ is measurable by
[[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Its signed integral is
defined by the positive and negative parts
([[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]],
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

maximum $1/e$ at $t=1/e$: $e=\exp(1)>1$ by
[[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], $1/e=\exp(-1)$ by
[[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], and $\log(1/e)=-1$ by
[[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and the inverse definition. The mean value
theorem gives increase before and decrease after this point
([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-integral-logarithm-derivative-and-normalisation]],
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]], [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).
At $t=0$ the negative part is zero. Since $Q$ is a probability measure,
$$\int \psi(r)^-\,dQ\le\frac1e.$$
The change-of-measure identity of [[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]],
applied to $\ell^-$ gives $\int\ell^-\,dP=\int\psi(r)^-\,dQ\le1/e$,
so $\int\ell\,dP$ is well-defined; applying it to both positive and negative
parts gives
$$D(P\|Q)=\int\ell\,dP=\int\psi(r)\,dQ=\int r\log r\,dQ,$$
with $0\log0:=0$ and a finite negative part. Therefore the extended integral
is well-defined without an $\infty-\infty$ ambiguity.

This convention is directional: the first argument must be absolutely
continuous with respect to the second for the integral formula to apply.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

derivations.claim: The reverse path density is strictly positive and finite at every finite path because every Gaussian variance is positive and each mean is finite. Its path marginal on $x_{1:T}$ is a probability density by successive integration of its reverse kernels and prior. For fixed $x_0$, the decoder density satisfies $p_\theta(x_0\mid x_1)\le(2\pi\sigma_1^2)^{-d/2}$, so integrating against that path marginal gives $p_\theta(x_0)<\infty$. It is strictly positive: on the positive-measure box $[-1,1]^{dT}$, the sets $\{p_\theta(x_{0:T})\ge1/n\}$ for positive integers $n$ cover the box because the density is positive everywhere. If all these sets had measure zero, their countable union would have measure zero, contradicting the positive measure of the box; one set therefore has positive measure, and the integral is positive. Thus $\pi_\theta(\cdot\mid x_0)$ is a proper positive density.

The forward path density is a probability density and is positive everywhere. Its log is the finite sum $\log q(x_{1:T}\mid x_0)=\sum_{t=1}^T\left[-\frac d2\log(2\pi\beta_t)-\frac{\|x_t-\sqrt{\alpha_t}x_{t-1}\|_2^2}{2\beta_t}\right]$. Under $q$, each normalized residual $(x_t-\sqrt{\alpha_t}x_{t-1})/\sqrt{\beta_t}$ has law $N_d(0,I_d)$ and finite second moment $d$ by [F10], so $\mathbb E_q|\log q|<\infty$. Since the reverse density is also positive everywhere, $\pi_\theta>0$ everywhere and the support condition $Q_{x_0}\ll\Pi_{\theta,x_0}$ holds.

Let $\gamma(x_{1:T})=p_\theta(x_{0:T})$ on path space with base measure $\lambda_{dT}$. Step 1.1 gives $Z=\int\gamma\,d\lambda_{dT}=p_\theta(x_0)\in(0,\infty)$ and the normalized target $\pi=\gamma/Z$; step 1.2 gives the support condition, and the Statement's integrability hypothesis together with step 1.2 gives $\mathbb E_q(|\log\gamma|+|\log q|)<\infty$. The direction is $Q_{x_0}\ll\Pi_{\theta,x_0}$, as required by [F8]. Therefore [F3], [F6], and [F9] apply, and [F4] gives the exact log-evidence identity and nonnegative reverse KL.

For $t\ge2$, the Markov property and positive Gaussian densities give $q(x_t\mid x_{t-1})=q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0)q(x_t\mid x_0)/q(x_{t-1}\mid x_0)$. Substitute this into $p_\theta(x_{0:T})/q(x_{1:T}\mid x_0)$. The ratios $q(x_{t-1}\mid x_0)/q(x_t\mid x_0)$ telescope, leaving $p_\theta(x_{0:T})/q(x_{1:T}\mid x_0)=[p(x_T)/q(x_T\mid x_0)]p_\theta(x_0\mid x_1)\prod_{t=2}^T p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)/q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0)$. Taking the $q$-expectation of the logarithm yields the stated endpoint-plus-step decomposition, with the t=1 term $-\mathbb E_{q(x_1\mid x_0)}\log p_\theta(x_0\mid x_1)$. Each reverse Gaussian log-density factor is bounded above; the assumed integrability of their finite sum makes each factor integrable, and the forward marginals and conditioned laws are Gaussian with finite quadratic moments, so the expectation splits termwise.

For $t\ge2$, substitute $x_t=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\epsilon$ into the posterior mean in [F2]. Using $\bar\alpha_t=\alpha_t\bar\alpha_{t-1}$ and $\beta_t=1-\alpha_t$ gives $\tilde\mu_t(x_t,x_0)=\frac1{\sqrt{\alpha_t}}\left(x_t-\frac{\beta_t}{\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}}\epsilon\right)$. The reverse mean is the same expression with $\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)$ in place of $\epsilon$, so $\|\tilde\mu_t-\mu_{\theta,t}\|_2^2=\frac{\beta_t^2}{\alpha_t(1-\bar\alpha_t)}\|\epsilon-\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)\|_2^2$. Both posterior and reverse variances are positive for $t\ge2$, so [F5] applies with $v=\tilde\beta_t$ and $w=\sigma_t^2$; it gives exactly the coefficient $w_t$ and constant $C_t$ in the Statement.

The terminal term remains $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q(x_T\mid x_0)\|N_d(0,I_d))$ in step 2.2 because finite $T$ and $0<\beta_t<1$ give $\bar\alpha_T>0$; the $t=1$ term remains the separate positive-variance decoder log-likelihood. For an explicit counterexample, take $d=1$, $T=2$, $\beta_1=\tfrac14$, $\beta_2=\tfrac12$, $\sigma_1^2=(2\pi)^{-1}$, and $\sigma_2^2=\tilde\beta_2=\tfrac15$. Then $\bar\alpha_1=\tfrac34$, $\bar\alpha_2=\tfrac38$, $w_2=\frac{(1/2)^2}{2(1/5)(1/2)(5/8)}=2$, and $C_2=\frac12(1-1+\log1)=0$. For a fixed datum $x_0$, set $\epsilon_\theta(x_1,1)=(x_1-\sqrt{3/4}\,x_0)/\sqrt{1/4}$ and $\epsilon_\theta(x_2,2)=(x_2-\sqrt{3/8}\,x_0)/\sqrt{5/8}+c$, with any $c\in\mathbb R$. These are finite Borel maps, and their Gaussian log densities have finite $q$-expectations because they are quadratic functions of finite-dimensional Gaussian variables. The first map makes $\mu_{\theta,1}(x_1)=x_0$, so the decoder density at its mean is $(2\pi\sigma_1^2)^{-1/2}=1$; integrating it against the normalized reverse path density gives $p_\theta(x_0)=1$ for every $c$. Under the forward chain, the $t=1$ noise error is zero and the $t=2$ error is $c$, so $L_{\mathrm{simple}}=c^2/2$, while the exact weighted $t=2$ ELBO contribution is $2c^2$ and its prior term is independent of $c$. Taking $c\ne0$ gives $L_{\mathrm{simple}}>0$ but exact negative log-likelihood $-\log p_\theta(x_0)=0$. Thus the unweighted loss is a surrogate, not in general the maximum-likelihood objective.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Let $d,T\ge1$ be finite integers, let $I_d$ be the $d\times d$ identity matrix, and let $\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_T\in(0,1)$. Set $\alpha_t=1-\beta_t$, $\bar\alpha_0=1$, and $\bar\alpha_t=\prod_{s=1}^t\alpha_s$. Write $\lambda_d$ for Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R^d$ and define, for $v>0$,
$$\phi_{d,v}(y;m)=(2\pi v)^{-d/2}\exp\!\left(-\frac{\|y-m\|_2^2}{2v}\right),\qquad y,m\in\mathbb R^d.$$
The notation $\|z\|_2^2=\sum_{i=1}^d z_i^2$ is the squared Euclidean norm. The displayed function is the Lebesgue density of $N_d(m,vI_d)$.

For each fixed $x_0\in\mathbb R^d$, the forward chain has path density on $(\mathbb R^d)^T$
$$q(x_{1:T}\mid x_0)=\prod_{t=1}^T \phi_{d,\beta_t}(x_t;\sqrt{\alpha_t}\,x_{t-1}).$$
Thus its transition from $x_{t-1}$ to $x_t$ is Gaussian with mean $\sqrt{\alpha_t}\,x_{t-1}$ and covariance $\beta_t I_d$. Each factor is a normalized density, and finite successive integration of the nonnegative product gives a probability density.

For a generic adjacent pair, the two model directions are shown below. The arrows indicate the direction in which each conditional density generates its target state; they assert no equality or inverse relation between the kernels.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=stealth]
  \node (previous) at (0,0) {$x_{t-1}$};
  \node (current) at (4,0) {$x_t$};
  \draw[->] (previous) to[bend left=24] node[midway,above] {$q(x_t\mid x_{t-1})$} (current);
  \draw[->] (current) to[bend left=24] node[midway,below] {$p_{\theta,t}(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)$} (previous);
\end{tikzpicture}
```

A learned reverse Gaussian model consists of finite-valued Borel maps $\mu_{\theta,t}:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ and fixed variances $\sigma_t^2\in(0,\infty)$, for $1\le t\le T$. It is the joint density
$$p_\theta(x_{0:T})=\phi_{d,1}(x_T;0)\prod_{t=1}^T\phi_{d,\sigma_t^2}(x_{t-1};\mu_{\theta,t}(x_t)).$$
Its prior is $p(x_T)=N_d(0,I_d)$, and its marginal density at $x_0$ is
$$p_\theta(x_0)=\int_{(\mathbb R^d)^T}p_\theta(x_{0:T})\,d\lambda_d(x_1)\cdots d\lambda_d(x_T),$$
whenever this integral is finite. The joint reverse density is normalized by successive integration of its Gaussian transition factors followed by the prior density.

For $t=1$, the forward-chain conditional $q(x_0\mid x_1,x_0)$ assigns probability one to every Borel set containing $x_0$ and zero to every Borel set not containing $x_0$; it is not a Lebesgue density. The separate learned reverse likelihood $p_\theta(x_0\mid x_1)$ is the Gaussian density above with variance $\sigma_1^2>0$.

Assume AC and the finite Gaussian forward chain with dimension $d\ge1$, horizon $T\ge1$, and schedule $0<\beta_t<1$ from the preceding definition. For each $x_0\in\mathbb R^d$ and $1\le t\le T$,
$$q(x_t\mid x_0)=N_d\!\left(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0,(1-\bar\alpha_t)I_d\right).$$
For every $2\le t\le T$, the conditional law given both endpoints is
$$q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0)=N_d\!\left(\frac{\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}\beta_t}{1-\bar\alpha_t}x_0+\frac{\sqrt{\alpha_t}(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})}{1-\bar\alpha_t}x_t,\ \tilde\beta_t I_d\right),\qquad \tilde\beta_t=\frac{\beta_t(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})}{1-\bar\alpha_t}>0.$$
The formula for $q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0)$ is only asserted for $t\ge2$; at $t=1$ the conditioning on $x_0$ makes $q(x_0\mid x_1,x_0)$ a point mass, not a Lebesgue density. The Gaussian conditional above does not assert that the unconditional reverse law $q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)$ is Gaussian.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

derivations.claim: The schedule gives $\alpha_1=1-\tfrac14=\tfrac34$, $\alpha_2=1-\tfrac12=\tfrac12$, $\bar\alpha_1=\tfrac34$, and $\bar\alpha_2=\tfrac34\cdot\tfrac12=\tfrac38$.
By [F2] and the scalar normal convention [F3], $q(x_2\mid x_0)$ has mean $\sqrt{3/8}\,x_0$ and variance $1-\tfrac38=\tfrac58$.

The posterior variance is $\tilde\beta_2=\frac{(1/2)(1-3/4)}{1-3/8}=\frac{1/8}{5/8}=\tfrac15$. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Let $d,T\ge1$ be finite integers, let $I_d$ be the $d\times d$ identity matrix, and let $\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_T\in(0,1)$. Set $\alpha_t=1-\beta_t$, $\bar\alpha_0=1$, and $\bar\alpha_t=\prod_{s=1}^t\alpha_s$. Write $\lambda_d$ for Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R^d$ and define, for $v>0$,
$$\phi_{d,v}(y;m)=(2\pi v)^{-d/2}\exp\!\left(-\frac{\|y-m\|_2^2}{2v}\right),\qquad y,m\in\mathbb R^d.$$
The notation $\|z\|_2^2=\sum_{i=1}^d z_i^2$ is the squared Euclidean norm. The displayed function is the Lebesgue density of $N_d(m,vI_d)$.

For each fixed $x_0\in\mathbb R^d$, the forward chain has path density on $(\mathbb R^d)^T$
$$q(x_{1:T}\mid x_0)=\prod_{t=1}^T \phi_{d,\beta_t}(x_t;\sqrt{\alpha_t}\,x_{t-1}).$$
Thus its transition from $x_{t-1}$ to $x_t$ is Gaussian with mean $\sqrt{\alpha_t}\,x_{t-1}$ and covariance $\beta_t I_d$. Each factor is a normalized density, and finite successive integration of the nonnegative product gives a probability density.

For a generic adjacent pair, the two model directions are shown below. The arrows indicate the direction in which each conditional density generates its target state; they assert no equality or inverse relation between the kernels.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=stealth]
  \node (previous) at (0,0) {$x_{t-1}$};
  \node (current) at (4,0) {$x_t$};
  \draw[->] (previous) to[bend left=24] node[midway,above] {$q(x_t\mid x_{t-1})$} (current);
  \draw[->] (current) to[bend left=24] node[midway,below] {$p_{\theta,t}(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)$} (previous);
\end{tikzpicture}
```

A learned reverse Gaussian model consists of finite-valued Borel maps $\mu_{\theta,t}:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ and fixed variances $\sigma_t^2\in(0,\infty)$, for $1\le t\le T$. It is the joint density
$$p_\theta(x_{0:T})=\phi_{d,1}(x_T;0)\prod_{t=1}^T\phi_{d,\sigma_t^2}(x_{t-1};\mu_{\theta,t}(x_t)).$$
Its prior is $p(x_T)=N_d(0,I_d)$, and its marginal density at $x_0$ is
$$p_\theta(x_0)=\int_{(\mathbb R^d)^T}p_\theta(x_{0:T})\,d\lambda_d(x_1)\cdots d\lambda_d(x_T),$$
whenever this integral is finite. The joint reverse density is normalized by successive integration of its Gaussian transition factors followed by the prior density.

For $t=1$, the forward-chain conditional $q(x_0\mid x_1,x_0)$ assigns probability one to every Borel set containing $x_0$ and zero to every Borel set not containing $x_0$; it is not a Lebesgue density. The separate learned reverse likelihood $p_\theta(x_0\mid x_1)$ is the Gaussian density above with variance $\sigma_1^2>0$.

Assume AC. Fix a finite Gaussian forward chain and reverse model as defined above, with finite-valued Borel reverse means and fixed variances $\sigma_t^2\in(0,\infty)$. For the noise-prediction parameterization, let $\epsilon_\theta:\mathbb R^d\times\{1,\ldots,T\}\to\mathbb R^d$ be Borel and set
$$\mu_{\theta,t}(x_t)=\frac1{\sqrt{\alpha_t}}\left(x_t-\frac{\beta_t}{\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}}\,\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)\right),\qquad 1\le t\le T.$$
For each fixed observed $x_0$, require $0<p_\theta(x_0)<\infty$, define the proper posterior density
$$\pi_\theta(x_{1:T}\mid x_0)=\frac{p_\theta(x_{0:T})}{p_\theta(x_0)},$$
and let $Q_{x_0}$ and $\Pi_{\theta,x_0}$ be the path probability measures with Lebesgue densities $q(x_{1:T}\mid x_0)$ and $\pi_\theta(x_{1:T}\mid x_0)$. Require $Q_{x_0}\ll\Pi_{\theta,x_0}$ and
$$\mathbb E_{q(\cdot\mid x_0)}\!\left[|\log q(x_{1:T}\mid x_0)|+|\log p_\theta(x_{0:T})|\right]<\infty.$$
Here $\mathbb E_q[f]$ means the integral of $f$ against the path law with density $q(\cdot\mid x_0)$. Define
$$\operatorname{ELBO}_\theta(x_0)=\mathbb E_q\!\left[\log p_\theta(x_{0:T})-\log q(x_{1:T}\mid x_0)\right].$$
Then
$$\log p_\theta(x_0)=\operatorname{ELBO}_\theta(x_0)+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q_{x_0}\|\Pi_{\theta,x_0}),\qquad D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q_{x_0}\|\Pi_{\theta,x_0})\ge0.$$
The negative ELBO has the exact decomposition
$$-\operatorname{ELBO}_\theta(x_0)=D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(q(x_T\mid x_0)\middle\|N_d(0,I_d)\right)+\mathbb E_{q(x_1\mid x_0)}[-\log p_\theta(x_0\mid x_1)]+\sum_{t=2}^T\mathbb E_{q(x_t\mid x_0)}\!\left[D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0)\middle\|p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)\right)\right].$$
In particular, for $t\ge2$, write
$$\tilde\mu_t(x_t,x_0)=\frac{\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}\beta_t}{1-\bar\alpha_t}x_0+\frac{\sqrt{\alpha_t}(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})}{1-\bar\alpha_t}x_t,\quad w_t=\frac{\beta_t^2}{2\sigma_t^2\alpha_t(1-\bar\alpha_t)},\quad C_t=\frac d2\left(\frac{\tilde\beta_t}{\sigma_t^2}-1+\log\frac{\sigma_t^2}{\tilde\beta_t}\right).$$
If $x_t=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\epsilon$ with $\epsilon\sim N_d(0,I_d)$, then the corresponding per-step KL term is
$$\mathbb E_\epsilon\!\left[w_t\left\|\epsilon-\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)\right\|_2^2+C_t\right].$$
At $t=1$, the reconstruction term is the separate learned likelihood $p_\theta(x_0\mid x_1)$ with variance $\sigma_1^2>0$; no Lebesgue density for $q(x_0\mid x_1,x_0)$ is used. For finite $T$, the terminal-prior KL is retained; no equality $q(x_T\mid x_0)=N_d(0,I_d)$ is assumed. The common unweighted objective
$$L_{\mathrm{simple}}(\theta;x_0)=\frac1T\sum_{t=1}^T\mathbb E_\epsilon\!\left[\left\|\epsilon-\epsilon_\theta\!\left(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\epsilon,t\right)\right\|_2^2\right]$$
drops the schedule weights and replaces the separate endpoint terms with noise-prediction losses, so it is not in general the exact maximum-likelihood objective.
